title: Why Did Xi Raise the Thucydides Trap With Trump and Putin?
h1: Xi raised the Thucydides Trap with Trump and Putin in Shenzhen. What does it mean?
question: Why did Xi Jinping raise the Thucydides Trap with Trump and Putin?
answer: To argue that war is a choice. Meeting Trump and Putin in Shenzhen on 19 November 2026, Xi said the three should move beyond the Thucydides Trap, the idea that a rising and a ruling power tend to slide into war. Xinhua quoted him saying it "is by no means inevitable". He raised it with Trump in May too.

event.name: Xi raises the Thucydides Trap at the China-Russia-US meeting in Shenzhen

artefact.text: NBC News's live blog of the Shenzhen meeting carries Xi's words as reported by Xinhua and the four points in the statements China and Russia released.
artefact.label: Read NBC News's live blog

timeline.text: Xi opens his Beijing summit with Trump by asking whether China and the United States can overcome the so-called Thucydides Trap, according to Euronews. Trump replies on Truth Social that Xi was referring to damage the United States suffered under his predecessor, Joe Biden.
In Shenzhen, on the sidelines of APEC, Xi tells Trump and Putin that the three countries should be partners, avoid conflict and move beyond the Thucydides Trap, NBC News reports, quoting Xinhua.
China and Russia release identical statements listing four points the leaders agreed, including reducing the risk of nuclear war. NBC News notes US officials did not immediately release a version.

mechanism.text: The Thucydides Trap is Graham Allison's name for the danger that a rising power's challenge to a ruling one ends in war, after Thucydides' account of Athens and Sparta. Euronews summarises his case file: 16 cases in 500 years where a rising power threatened an established one, 12 of which ended in war.

mechanism.h: Xi used it to argue the outcome is a choice
mechanism.text: In Shenzhen Xi did not say war was coming. Xinhua, quoted by NBC News, has him saying the trap "is by no means inevitable. The key lies in the choices made by major powers." Euronews notes he has used the concept since 2013 to argue that war is not inevitable if both sides show restraint. The name is invoked to describe the risk and, in the same breath, to say it can be avoided.

mechanism.h: The meeting's text addressed the risk the trap names
mechanism.text: The Jerusalem Post reports a four-point declaration in which the leaders reaffirmed that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought", and Xinhua quoted Xi asking the three not to challenge one another's red lines. Those are the kinds of commitments meant to keep a rivalry short of war. The same report says the declaration set no specific arms reductions and no timetable for talks.

mechanism.h: Each side reads the frame its own way
mechanism.text: In May, Euronews reports, Trump read Xi's reference as a comment on American decline and placed that decline in the Biden years. That is the trap's own framing at work: one side cast as rising and one as ruling, and each leader answering for which role it is given. We describe the framing here; we take no view on which reading is right.

limits: A leader naming the trap is not evidence that war is more or less likely. It shows how Xi frames the relationship in public, not what the three governments will do.

The concept is contested. Euronews notes academic criticism of Allison's case selection, including the peaceful handover of leadership from Britain to the United States, which it says he excluded. Writing in the Lowy Institute's Interpreter, Shameek Godara calls the frame "dangerously incomplete" for a rivalry fought over trade, chips and standards as much as territory.

The record of what was agreed is one-sided so far. NBC News reports that the four points come from identical Chinese and Russian statements and that US officials did not immediately release their own version.

Allison's trap is about a pair of powers, one rising and one ruling. Shenzhen was a three-way meeting, and the concept by itself says nothing about where Russia fits. That is our reading, not a claim from the sources.

faqs.a: Graham Allison's name for the danger of war when a rising power threatens to displace a ruling one, after Thucydides' history of Athens and Sparta. His case file counts 16 such rivalries in 500 years, 12 of which ended in war, according to Euronews.

faqs.q: Did Xi say the US and China are headed for war?
faqs.a: No. Xinhua, quoted by NBC News, reports him saying the trap "is by no means inevitable" and that "the key lies in the choices made by major powers". He used the name to argue the risk can be avoided.

faqs.q: What did the Shenzhen meeting agree?
faqs.a: According to identical statements from China and Russia, reported by NBC News, four points: reform at the United Nations, more refined oil production and supply, a warning to the International Criminal Court and similar bodies, and reducing the risk of nuclear war. The Jerusalem Post says the declaration set no specific arms reductions or timetable.

faqs.q: Has Xi raised the trap before?
faqs.a: Yes. Euronews reports he opened his May 2026 Beijing summit with Trump by asking whether the two countries could overcome it, and that he has used the concept since 2013.

predictions.text: By 31 December 2027, Xi will raise the Thucydides Trap again in a meeting or call with a US president, as reported by Xinhua or a major international outlet. This is wrong if no such report appears by that date.

actions: When a leader names the Thucydides Trap, check whether they say war is likely or say it can be avoided. Xi has used it for the second.
Read Allison's 12-in-16 figure as a count from a chosen set of cases, and look at which cases critics say were left out.
For what a summit agreed, look for each side's own text. Here only China and Russia had published theirs when this was written.
whyItMatters: The Thucydides Trap is one of the few named ideas heads of state use about each other in public. In Shenzhen it framed a three-way meeting of the Chinese, American and Russian leaders that NBC News called historic, and Xi used it to say the outcome depends on choices, not on fate.
